full_judgment:
17. The earliest view in this connection which has been placed before us is the view of a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court, as reported in the case of Kunj Behari Lal Vs. Bharagava Commercial Bank, which has been relied upon on behalf of the respondents in this case. The learned Judges of the Allahabad High Court have taken the view that the notice of the sale, as has been referred to in section 176 of the Contract Act, means the notice of the intention to sell and does not necessarily mean that a sale should be arranged and due notice of all the details should be given to the pawner. According to the learned Judges, it is quite clear that the intention of the law is that the pawnee should give the pawner a reasonable time within which he exercises his right to redeem, and then proceed to sell the property, if not redeemed. It has been further observed in the said Allahabad case that the provision of section 176 does not contemplate that the pawnee should give the pawnor information of the actual date, time and place of the sale. It appears that this decision of the Allahabad High Court has been the basis of a number of subsequent judicial views and it has been followed in the cases of Cocanada Vs. Gundabathula Suryanarayanamurty and another, A.I.R. 1920 Madras 1022, same case 114 I.C. 820, Cooverje Umersey Vs. Mawji Vaghji and another in A.I.R. 1937 Bom. 26, Hulas Kunwar Vs. Allahabad Bank Limited, A.I.R. 1958 Cal. 644 and also in the judgment of Mehar Singh, J. in Messrs. Grison Knitting Works Vs. Laxmi commercial Bank Ltd. and others, A.I.R. 1960 Punjab 98. Although no case law was referred to, the same principle as laid down by a Division Bench of the West Pakistan High Court in the case of Messrs continental sundicate of Trade Vs. Lloyds Bank Ltd. P.L.D. 1966 (W.P) Karachi 556. 

 20. In the case of Hulas Kunwar Vs. Allahabad bank Ltd A.I.R. 1958 Cal. 644, a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court appears to have taken a view which is not consistent with me view taken in the earlier cast reported in 36 C.W.N. 263. Although in the later Calcutta case, (A.I.R 1958 Cal. 644) the view has been expressed more or less in the same line as in the Allahabad case but the facts of the Calcutta case have some distinguishable features. In the said case the question arose in connection with the sale of certain shares which were pledged by way of security of the debt and it was pointed out therein that it was very difficult to notify the exact date of the sale of the shares in advance, as such shares were to be sold in a fluctuating market at a time when the most favorable price could be obtained. 

 It appears that the right of sale which has been conferred upon the pawnee by the aforesaid provision arises on default of the pawnor in payment of the debt at the stipulated time of the promise, and after the accrued of the right to sell, the pawnee shall have to give a reasonable notice of the sale. This language is, in our opinion, sufficiently clear to indicate that what the pawnee is required under this provision is to give a reasonable notice of the sale and not a notice of the mere intention to sell, as has been held in the Allahabad case referred to above. To read 'intention to sell' in place of 'the sale' is reading something in the statute, which is not there, and according to the well-established cannot of interpretation of statutes such a manner of reading is very much disapproved'. There is no doubt that the court may in interpretation a statute under certain circumstances, add a word or even leave out a word, if such a reading is found necessary to avoid a kind of absurdity, inconsistency or injustice which may be presumed to have not been intended by the lawmaker. What a court is required to do in interpreting a statute is to find out the legislative intent of the law maker. Ordinarily, the literal run of interpretation of the statutes is to be followed and the intention of the legislature is to be found out from the words actually used by the law maker in the statute. If the literal rule of interpretation leads is to some kind of inconsistency or absurdity or injustice, the court has certainly power to modify the language of the statutory provision in order to bring it in accord with the legislative intent. But in the present case we do not find any such absurdity, inconsistency of injustice, and therefore there is no valid reason for departing from the literal rule of interpretation and for adding certain words to the statutory provision, which are not there. It appears to us that the view expressed by Tek Chand, J as to the use of the word 'the' before the word 'sale', which did not find favor with the learned Judges of the Calcutta High Court in Hulas Kunwar's case reported in A.I.R. 1958 Calcutta 644, is quite reasonable. In our opinion the words "reason" able notice of the sale" clearly refer to the particulars of the sale which is going to be held by the pawnee in exercise of his right and they do not mean merely the pawnee's intention of sale. 

 28. We may, however, observe that under certain circumstances it may be extremely difficult to notify the actual date of the sale beforehand and have already noticed, while discussing the case reported in AIR 1958 Cal. 644, that in the facts of that particular case it might have been difficult to intimate the exact time of the sale consistently with the interests of the parties concerned, but sufficient particulars as to the actual sale could be given in such a case in order to enable the pawnor to take appropriate step to protect his own interest.
